query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled phase‐selective annealing treatment that promotes partial recrystallization of the ductile phase in the lamellar eutectic HEA will alleviate dislocation pile‐ups at the internal phase boundaries, reducing local stress concentrations and microcrack initiation, thereby overcoming brittleness and limited ductility while maintaining or increasing the overall strength.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure (e.g., a combination of a soft, ductile FCC phase and a hard B2 or L12 phase) that exhibits dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries, leading to local stress concentrations and microcracking under room-temperature tensile loading.
generation.intervention: Apply a tailored, phase-selective annealing heat treatment (e.g., at around 700°C for a controlled, short duration in an inert atmosphere) designed to recrystallize and refine the grain structure of the ductile phase while preserving the hard phase morphology.
generation.conditions: Heat treatment performed under inert (argon) atmosphere at approximately 700°C for a predetermined short time to induce selective recrystallization; subsequent room-temperature tensile testing under quasi-static deformation (strain rate ~10^-3 s^-1) to assess mechanical performance.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined, recrystallized ductile phase with reduced and more uniformly distributed grain boundaries, which minimizes dislocation pile-up at the interphase interfaces while maintaining a fine lamellar arrangement with the hard phases.
generation.mechanism: The selective annealing treatment enables recovery and partial recrystallization of the ductile (e.g., FCC) phase, thereby redistributing and reducing accumulated dislocations at the phase interfaces. This relieves local stress concentrations that otherwise lead to microcrack nucleation, while the preserved hard phase continues to impede dislocation motion, ensuring high strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: The treated HEA is expected to exhibit a significant improvement in uniform tensile ductility (likely an increase in elongation relative to the untreated state) without compromising—and potentially even increasing—the yield and ultimate tensile strength, compared to the starting material.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic HEA with a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar microstructure that suffers from dislocation pile-ups at phase boundaries, causing local stress concentrations, microcracking, and brittle failure under room-temperature tensile loading.
generation.boundary: The benefit of the treatment is contingent upon the precise control of annealing temperature and time; excessive coarsening or over-recrystallization of the hard phase could undermine strength, while insufficient treatment may not adequately relieve dislocation pile-ups.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies indicate that controlled phase-selective annealing can improve ductility in similar eutectic HEAs, the optimal parameters for simultaneously enhancing ductility and strength in this specific system require experimental validation. The quantitative improvement in ductility (e.g., percent elongation gain) and potential trade-offs in strength are not fully predictable without further study.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same as-cast eutectic HEA. Subject one set to the proposed phase-selective annealing treatment (e.g., 700°C for a controlled time under argon) designed to recrystallize the ductile phase, while keeping the other set as the untreated control. Characterize the microstructure (using SEM, TEM, EBSD) to assess the extent of recrystallization and interphase boundary modifications. Perform room-temperature quasi-static tensile tests on both sets to compare yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and uniform elongation.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (grain size, recrystallized fraction, dislocation density near phase boundaries)
Mechanical properties: yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, uniform elongation from tensile tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in ductility (uniform elongation) without a loss in strength compared to the control, or if the microstructural analyses demonstrate persistent dislocation pile-ups and similar boundary characteristics as in the untreated material, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. Recent studies indicate that eutectic high-entropy alloys can simultaneously possess high strength and high ductility, which have potential industrial applications. The present study focuses on Al0.7CoCrFeNi, a lamellar dual-phase (fcc + B2) precipitation-strengthenable eutectic high entropy alloy. This alloy exhibits an fcc + B2 (B2 with bcc nano-precipitates) microstructure resulting in a combination of the soft and ductile fcc phase together with hard B2 phase. Low temperature annealing leads to the precipitation of ordered L12 intermetallic precipitates within the fcc resulting in enhanced strength. The strengthening contribution due to fine scale L12 is modeled using Orowan dislocation bowing and by-pass mechanism. The alloy was tested under quasi-static (strain-rate = 10−3 s−1) tensile loading and dynamic (strain-rate = 103 s−1) compressive loading. Due to the fine lamellar microstructure with a large number of fcc-bcc interfaces, the alloy show relatively high flow-stresses, ~1400 MPa under quasi-static loading and in excess of 1800 MPa under dynamic loading. Excellent ductility is crucial not only for shaping but also for strengthening metals and alloys. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys are suffering from the limited ductility and losing competitiveness among advanced structural materials. Here we report a distinctive concept of phase-selective recrystallization to overcome this challenge for eutectic alloys by triggering the strain hardening capacity of the duplex phases completely. We manipulate the strain partitioning behavior of the two phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to obtain the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in the skeleton of a hard phase. The resulting microstructure fully releases the strain hardening capacity in EHEA by eliminating the weak boundaries. Our phase-selectively recrystallized EHEA achieves a high ductility of ∼35% uniform elongation with true stress of ∼2 GPa. This concept is universal for various duplex alloys with soft and hard phases and opens new frontiers for traditional eutectic alloys as high-strength metallic materials.
